progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: C1 to C9 and Year 11 (P02 colourimetry is an optional branch and is not relied on): dynamic equilibrium with both directions going at equal rates (C1); the K expression and its rules, with pure solids, pure liquids and the solvent water left out, and the size bands (C5); K changes only with temperature (C9); acids release hydrogen ions in water and react with magnesium to make hydrogen; scientific notation. Not assumed: pH, Bronsted-Lowry theory, conjugate pairs, any Module 6 content.
progression.startsWith: Two beakers of acid at the same concentration with the same magnesium, one fizzing hard and one slowly, and the question of what equilibrium and which K explain the difference.
progression.stopsAfter: Explaining the difference between a strong acid (ionises completely) and a weak acid (molecules and ions in balance); writing Ka for HA = H+ + A- and for HA + H2O = H3O+ + A- with water left out; writing Kb for ammonia with water left out; ranking weak acids by Ka (powers of ten first) and saying what a bigger Ka means at equilibrium at the same concentration; saying that Ka is not [H+] or pH; writing Ksp for a 1 : 1 solid as the same rule. No pH, pKa, Kw, Ka x Kb = Kw, conjugate pairs, weak-acid ICE tables, Ksp calculations or Gibbs free energy.
progression.nextLesson: C11: how an ionic solid dissolves in water.

teaching.task: Write Ka and Kb as ordinary K expressions with water and solids left out, and use their size to compare weak acids.
teaching.causalExplanation: The bubbles come from hydrogen ions. Hydrochloric acid molecules all split into ions, so it is a strong acid. Acetic acid molecules split and the ions join back up, the two directions balance while most molecules are still whole, so far fewer hydrogen ions meet the magnesium. A balance of molecules and ions is an equilibrium, so it has a K written by the rule already known; Ka is only its name. Water is the solvent in a huge steady amount, so it stays out. A small Ka means a small top and a big bottom, so mostly whole molecules; at the same concentration a bigger Ka means more split into ions. A strong acid leaves essentially no molecules for the bottom, so no Ka value is used. Ammonia and silver chloride follow the same rule with the solvent and the pure solid left out.
teaching.conversationalApproach: Opens on two painted beakers at the same concentration with different fizz, uses particle lenses to explain strong and weak, builds the Ka expression from the known rule, shows water left out in a tray, reads the size on a log strip, handles strong acids, ammonia and silver chloride as the same rule, gives one memory aid, then asks two unseen demands with a short pause and feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: Same acid concentration, same metal, different fizz. Why, and which K tells you?
teaching.understandingCheck: Methanoic acid has Ka 1.8 x 10^-4 and hydrogen cyanide has Ka 6.2 x 10^-10, both at 25 C: write Ka for HCN(aq) + H2O(l) = H3O+(aq) + CN-(aq) (water left out), and say which is the stronger acid and why (methanoic acid, about three hundred thousand times bigger Ka, powers of ten first).
teaching.curriculumScope: Explore the use of Keq for different types of reactions, including dissociation of acids and bases, with ionic dissociation introduced as the same rule (Module 5, p1082 to p1084). pH, pKa, Kw, conjugate pairs, weak-acid ICE tables, Ksp calculations and Gibbs free energy are deferred.

design.visualSystem: Explainer engine: warm paper stage, handwritten Caveat headings, amber doodle layer, the painted strong and weak acid magnesium beakers, vinegar bottle and saturated beaker, coded particle lenses, the extended C5 expression builder with a left-out tray, a coded log size strip, and the C9 100-square grids. Colour key: H+ and H3O+ amber, acid anion violet, whole acid molecules navy, OH- green, NH4+ violet, water pale blue, K teal, anything left out of K greyed in the tray.
design.transitionPlan: The two beakers anchor the hook and stay in the left column while particle lenses open above them; the equation strip sits above the builder in every scene; the tray makes each exclusion visible; the size strip carries acetic acid, hydrofluoric acid and later the attempt markers; the HCl lens returns for strong acids; ammonia and the saturated beaker reuse the lens and tray; the three expressions line up for the aid; the attempt board clears the aids and the feedback rebuilds the builder and the strip; the next chip slides in; scene crossfade with settle.
